班東尼琴屬六角手風琴的日耳曼體系，由德國樂器商海因里希·班命名，1850年班東尼: The bandoneon belongs to the German system of concertinas, and is named after the German instrument maker Heinrich Band; the Band system was established in 1850, and the instrument was originally for religious and popular music. Around 1870 German and Italian emigrants and sailors brought it to Argentina, where it entered tango music, which grew out of the milonga, and was used for chamamé as well. From 1910 Germany produced for the Argentine and Uruguayan market, and in 1930 25,000 instruments were shipped to Argentina; mass production ended after the Second World War. Arolas and Greco brought it into tango, and Maffia and Laurenz developed the sextet line-up. A single-note variant appeared in the 1920s, and in 2014 the National University of Lanús promoted affordable domestic production.
班東尼琴屬氣鳴樂器，H-S 412.132。演奏時以雙手夾持琴身，推拉風箱使氣流: The bandoneon is an aerophone, H-S 412.132. It is held between both hands, and pushing and pulling the bellows sends air through the reeds while the buttons select the notes; the buttons move in the same direction as the bellows, unlike the perpendicular keys of the accordion. For a beginner the key point is the bisonoric reed system: the same button gives a different note on push and on pull, and the left and right hands each have open and closed key positions, four layouts in all. Many tango players play almost entirely on the pull, and when necessary use the air-release button to close the bellows quickly and return to pulling.
班東尼琴屬氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 412.132。演奏: The bandoneon is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 412.132. The player holds the body between both hands, pulling and pushing the bellows so that air passes the tuned metal reeds, and selects the notes with the buttons. Unlike most accordions it usually has no register switches, and the expression comes mainly from the bellows pressure and the buttons. The two hands differ in timbre: the wooden case on the left makes the left hand muffled and nasal, while the right is brighter and sharper. It uses a bisonoric reed system, so the same button gives a different note on push and on pull; the common Rheinische system has 71 buttons and 142 notes, and can play in every key. The buttons move parallel to the bellows, unlike the perpendicular keys of the accordion, and this also makes its timbre and handling different from the single-note variants.

In the sextet of a typical tango orchestra it usually forms a section of two bandoneons. It can be heard in the playing and arranging of Ástor Piazzolla, whose 1969 work Fugata presents it directly.

The bandoneon is an aerophone of the concertina family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 412.132. The player holds the body between both hands, sends air past the tuned metal reeds by pushing and pulling the bellows, and selects the notes with the buttons. Unlike most accordions it usually has no register switches, and the two hands differ in timbre because of the wooden cases. The bandoneon is common in the tango ensembles of Argentina and Uruguay and is also used in music such as chamamé; its buttons mostly use a bisonoric reed system, so that pushing and pulling give different notes.
